deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. On the previous page Gauss solves the direct geodetic problem on the ellipsoid: given the latitude φ of a station, the azimuth ζ of a line and its length s, find the end latitude φ', the end azimuth ζ' and the longitude difference λ. He uses a worked example with log s = 5.3586, about 228 km, and compares his results with the formulas Delambre used for the French survey. This page gives a second solution through an auxiliary sphere in reduced (parametric) latitude. Notation: a is the semi-major axis, e the eccentricity, and Gauss writes sin φ^2 for sin²φ.

A. Relations for the reduced latitude ψ.
(i) tan ψ = √(1−e²) tan φ.
(ii) cos ψ = cos φ/√(1−e² sin²φ). This follows from cos²ψ = 1/(1+(1−e²)tan²φ) = cos²φ/(1−e² sin²φ).
(iii) sin ψ = tan ψ cos ψ = √((1−e²)/(1−e² sin²φ)) · sin φ.
(iv) Differentiating (i): sec²ψ dψ = √(1−e²) sec²φ dφ. Hence dψ = dφ · (cos ψ sin ψ)/(cos φ sin φ) = dφ · √(1−e²)/(1−e² sin²φ).

B. 'The above problem can also be solved thus' (pencil note by Krüger: Werke Band IX p.122).
Setup (my explanation). Work on a sphere where the starting point A has latitude ψ. S is the spherical arc corresponding to s. From the μ term below it is implicitly S² = (s²/a²)(1−e² sin²φ)/(1−e²), i.e. S = s/(a√(1−e² cos²ψ)), which is Bessel's scale factor taken at the initial point.
Triangle PAB has pole P and end point B, with ζ counted from the meridian direction away from the pole. Drop the perpendicular from B onto the meridian of A; call its foot D and set u = AD.

Right triangle ABD (hypotenuse S, angle ζ at A), by Napier's rules:
(2) tan u = tan S cos ζ.
(6) tan p = tan ζ cos S, where p = 90° − ∠ABD.
The perpendicular h = BD satisfies tan h = sin u tan ζ = tan S sin p, and sin h = sin S sin ζ.

Right triangle PDB. D has latitude ψ−u, the angle at P is the spherical longitude L, and the end point has reduced latitude ψ'.
(3) tan L = tan h / cos(ψ−u) = sin u tan ζ / cos(ψ−u) = tan S sin p / cos(ψ−u).
(4) tan ψ' = tan(ψ−u) cos L.
(7) tan q = tan(ψ−u) sin ζ sin S = tan L sin ψ'. Here q = 90° − ∠PBD.

Returning to the ellipsoid:
(5) tan φ' = tan ψ'/√(1−e²).
(8) ζ' = q − p. This is the angle PBA expressed as a difference of complements; the sign follows Gauss's azimuth convention.
(9) λ = L √((1−e²)/(1−e² sin²φ)) = L √(1−e² cos²ψ). This is Bessel's dλ = √(1−e² cos²ψ) dω, with the factor frozen at the initial latitude.

C. Series approximations ('so ist hinlänglich genau').
Define w by tan(ψ−u) = √(1−e²) tan(φ−w), so that φ−w is the geodetic latitude of the foot point D. Then w = (4)·A·s·cos ζ, where A (defined on an earlier page) is essentially 1/(meridian radius) in seconds.
The correction factor is log(4) = (1/3)(s²/a²)(1−e² sin²φ)/(1−e²) − (1/3)w²(1−e² sin²φ)²/(1−e²) = μ − ν, with natural logarithms. This comes from expanding arctan(tan S cos ζ) = S cos ζ (1 + S²/3 − u²/3 + …), with μ = S²/3 and ν ≈ u²/3.
Similarly p = ζ − ½(5)·(s²/a²)·(1−e² sin²φ)/(1−e²)·cos ζ sin ζ = ζ − ½(5) S² sin ζ cos ζ, with log(5) = ½μ − ¾ν.
errors: Relations (i)-(iv) are correct. The two expressions for dψ agree, since both equal √(1−e²)/(1−e² sin²φ).
Steps (2), (3) (both forms), (4), (6) and the corrected (7) are exact consequences of Napier's rules in the two right spherical triangles; I verified the identity tan L·sin ψ' = tan(ψ−u)·sin h.
In (7) Gauss first wrote tan ψ and then corrected it to tan(ψ−u). Only the corrected version is right.

(8) gives ζ' as q − p. The geometric angle PBA has magnitude |p − q| in this configuration, so the sign and orientation depend on Gauss's azimuth convention (ζ counted from the direction away from the pole). This is not an error, but it is not stated on the page.
(9) and the implicit scale S = s/(a√(1−e²cos²ψ)) evaluate Bessel's variable factor √(1−e²cos²ψ) only at the initial point. This is an approximation valid for short lines, not an exact transformation.

Apparent slip in log(5). Expanding the exact relation tan p = tan ζ cos S gives ζ − p = ½S² sin ζ cos ζ·(1 − S²/12 + ½S² sin²ζ + …). Hence log(5) = (5/4)μ − (3/2)ν, not ½μ − ¾ν. Gauss's expression has the correct constant term (−S²/12) but only half the S² sin²ζ term. Numerically, at ζ = 45° and S = 0.1 the discrepancy is about 0.65″; at the scale of the 228 km example it is about 0.01″.

Possible slip in ν. Since u ≈ w·dψ/dφ = w√(1−e²)/(1−e² sin²φ), one expects ν = (1/3)u² = (1/3)w²(1−e²)/(1−e² sin²φ)². Gauss writes the reciprocal ellipsoidal factor (1−e² sin²φ)²/(1−e²). The difference is of relative order e² within a third-order term, so it is practically negligible ('hinlänglich genau'). It could also reflect a different normalisation of w defined elsewhere.

results.what: Reduced (parametric) latitude ψ with tan ψ = √(1−e²) tan φ, the expressions for cos ψ and sin ψ, and dψ/dφ = √(1−e²)/(1−e² sin²φ)
results.usually_credited_to: Legendre (1806) and Bessel (1825/26) for the geodetic use; the relations themselves are classical

results.what: Direct geodetic problem solved by mapping to an auxiliary sphere in reduced latitude, splitting the triangle by a perpendicular onto the initial meridian (Napier's rules), then converting back with λ = L√(1−e²cos²ψ) and S = s/(a√(1−e²cos²ψ)) frozen at the initial point
results.modern_name: Bessel's auxiliary-sphere method for the direct geodetic problem (short-line simplified form)
results.usually_credited_to: F. W. Bessel, Astronomische Nachrichten 1825/26; precursors Legendre and Oriani

results.what: Series corrections: w = A s cos ζ·exp(μ−ν) and p = ζ − ½S² sin ζ cos ζ·exp(½μ−¾ν), with μ = S²/3 and ν ≈ u²/3
results.modern_name: Taylor/Legendre-type series for the direct problem (arctan expansions)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard geodetic series practice (Legendre, Delambre, Bessel, Gauss)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a working note on the direct geodetic problem using reduced latitude and an auxiliary sphere, a technique made standard by Bessel (1826) and familiar from Legendre and Oriani. Krüger's pencil reference shows the material was printed in Gauss's Werke IX p.122, so it is already known as Gauss's. The only non-routine features are small slips in the series coefficients.

transcription_corrections: Step 7: in the image Gauss crossed out 'tang ψ' and wrote '(ψ−u)' above it. The intended formula is tan q = tan(ψ−u)·sin ζ·sin S = tan L·sin ψ'.
Step 3: the second sign is an ordinary '=' with a dot above (≐), meaning 'equivalently'. Both forms are equal, not approximations of each other.
The pencil note 'band IX p.122' (Krüger's hand, matching the 'Kr' in the left margin) refers to Gauss Werke vol. IX p.122, where this material is printed.
Step 2 should read tan u = tan S · cos ζ ('tg.S.' is Gauss's abbreviation for tang S).
Next to step 8 there is a heavily struck-out scribble, followed by a double vertical rule enclosing steps 8 and 9. It is not part of the formulas.
